<STRUCT_0001>
We choose a big fppf site <MATH_0001>.
All schemes are contained in <MATH_0002>.
And all rings <MATH_0003> considered have the property that
<MATH_0004> is (isomorphic) to an object of this big site.

<STRUCT_0002><STRUCT_0003>
We also fix a base scheme <MATH_0005>, by the conventions above an element
of <MATH_0006>. The reader who is only interested
in the absolute case can take <MATH_0007>.

<STRUCT_0004><STRUCT_0005>
Here are our conventions regarding algebraic stacks:
<STRUCT_0006>
<STRUCT_0007> When we say <TEXTITOPEN_0001>algebraic stack<TEXTITCLOSE_0001> we will mean an algebraic
stacks over <MATH_0008>, i.e., a category fibred in groupoids
<MATH_0009>
which satisfies the conditions of
Algebraic Stacks, Definition <REF_0001>.
<STRUCT_0008> We will say <MATH_0010> is a
<TEXTITOPEN_0002>morphism of algebraic stacks<TEXTITCLOSE_0002> to indicate a <MATH_0011>-morphism
of algebraic stacks over <MATH_0012>, i.e., a <MATH_0013>-morphism of categories fibred
in groupoids over <MATH_0014>, see
Algebraic Stacks,
Definition <REF_0002>.
<STRUCT_0009> A <TEXTITOPEN_0003><MATH_0015>-morphism<TEXTITCLOSE_0003> <MATH_0016> will
indicate a <MATH_0017>-morphism in the <MATH_0018>-category of algebraic stacks over
<MATH_0019>, see
Algebraic Stacks,
Definition <REF_0003>.
<STRUCT_0010> Given morphisms <MATH_0020>
and <MATH_0021> of algebraic stacks
we abusively call the <MATH_0022>-fibre product
<MATH_0023> the <TEXTITOPEN_0004>fibre product<TEXTITCLOSE_0004>.
<STRUCT_0011> We will write <MATH_0024> for the
product of the algebraic stacks <MATH_0025>, <MATH_0026>.
<STRUCT_0012> We will often abuse notation and say two algebraic stacks
<MATH_0027> and <MATH_0028> are <TEXTITOPEN_0005>isomorphic<TEXTITCLOSE_0005> if they are
equivalent in this <MATH_0029>-category.
<STRUCT_0013>
Here are our conventions regarding algebraic spaces.
<STRUCT_0014>
<STRUCT_0015> If we say <MATH_0030> is an <TEXTITOPEN_0006>algebraic space<TEXTITCLOSE_0006> then we mean that
<MATH_0031> is an algebraic space over <MATH_0032>, i.e., <MATH_0033> is a presheaf on
<MATH_0034> which satisfies the conditions of
Spaces, Definition <REF_0004>.
<STRUCT_0016> A <TEXTITOPEN_0007>morphism of algebraic spaces<TEXTITCLOSE_0007> <MATH_0035> is a morphism
of algebraic spaces over <MATH_0036> as defined in
Spaces, Definition <REF_0005>.
<STRUCT_0017> We will <TEXTBFOPEN_0001>not<TEXTBFCLOSE_0001> distinguish between an algebraic space <MATH_0037>
and the algebraic stack <MATH_0038>
it gives rise to, see
Algebraic Stacks, Lemma <REF_0006>.
<STRUCT_0018> In particular, a <TEXTITOPEN_0008>morphism<TEXTITCLOSE_0008> <MATH_0039> from <MATH_0040>
to an algebraic stack <MATH_0041> means a morphism
<MATH_0042> of algebraic stacks.
Similarly for morphisms <MATH_0043>.
<STRUCT_0019> Moreover, given an algebraic stack <MATH_0044> we say
<TEXTITOPEN_0009><MATH_0045> is an algebraic space<TEXTITCLOSE_0009> to indicate that <MATH_0046>
is representable by an algebraic space, see
Algebraic Stacks,
Definition <REF_0007>.
<STRUCT_0020> We will use the following notational convention: If we
indicate an algebraic stack by a roman capital
(such as <MATH_0047>) then it will be the case that
its inertia stack is trivial, and hence it is an algebraic space, see
Algebraic Stacks,
Proposition <REF_0008>.
<STRUCT_0021>
Here are our conventions regarding schemes.
<STRUCT_0022>
<STRUCT_0023> If we say <MATH_0048> is a <TEXTITOPEN_0010>scheme<TEXTITCLOSE_0010> then we mean that
<MATH_0049> is a scheme over <MATH_0050>, i.e., <MATH_0051> is an object of <MATH_0052>.
<STRUCT_0024> By a <TEXTITOPEN_0011>morphism of schemes<TEXTITCLOSE_0011> we mean a morphism of schemes over <MATH_0053>.
<STRUCT_0025> We will <TEXTBFOPEN_0002>not<TEXTBFCLOSE_0002> distinguish between a scheme <MATH_0054> and the
algebraic stack <MATH_0055> it gives rise
to, see
Algebraic Stacks, Lemma <REF_0009>.
<STRUCT_0026> In particular, a <TEXTITOPEN_0012>morphism<TEXTITCLOSE_0012> <MATH_0056> from
a scheme <MATH_0057> to an algebraic stack <MATH_0058> means a morphism
<MATH_0059> of algebraic stacks.
Similarly for morphisms <MATH_0060>.
<STRUCT_0027> Moreover, given an algebraic stack <MATH_0061> we say
<TEXTITOPEN_0013><MATH_0062> is a scheme<TEXTITCLOSE_0013> to indicate that <MATH_0063>
is representable, see
Algebraic Stacks, Section <REF_0010>.
<STRUCT_0028>
Here are our conventions regarding morphisms of algebraic stacks:
<STRUCT_0029>
<STRUCT_0030> A morphism <MATH_0064>
of algebraic stacks is <TEXTITOPEN_0014>representable<TEXTITCLOSE_0014>, or
<TEXTITOPEN_0015>representable by schemes<TEXTITCLOSE_0015> if for every scheme
<MATH_0065> and morphism <MATH_0066> the fibre product
<MATH_0067> is a scheme.
See
Algebraic Stacks, Section <REF_0011>.
<STRUCT_0031> A morphism <MATH_0068>
of algebraic stacks is <TEXTITOPEN_0016>representable by algebraic spaces<TEXTITCLOSE_0016>
if for every scheme <MATH_0069> and morphism <MATH_0070> the fibre product
<MATH_0071> is an algebraic space.
See Algebraic Stacks,
Definition <REF_0012>.
In this case <MATH_0072> is an algebraic
space whenever <MATH_0073> is a morphism whose source is
an algebraic space, see
Algebraic Stacks,
Lemma <REF_0013>.
<STRUCT_0032> We may abuse notation and say that a diagram of algebraic stacks
commutes if the diagram is <MATH_0074>-commutative in the <MATH_0075>-category of
algebraic stacks.
<STRUCT_0033>
Note that every morphism <MATH_0076> from an algebraic space
to an algebraic stack is representable by algebraic spaces, see
Algebraic Stacks, Lemma <REF_0014>.
We will use this basic result without further mention.
